headline: High: shared filesystem and broad tool/network access make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A reads/writes the user filesystem and uses MCP; Agent B also reads local/mounted files and supports MCP/tool calling. That creates a direct content bridge where attacker-controlled files or tool outputs from either side can be treated as instructions. No provenance or isolation is documented, so the safer higher severity is warranted.
conditions: IF Agent B ingests files produced by Agent A without provenance checks, prompt injection is possible.
IF either agent parses shared file contents as instructions, the bridge becomes exploitable.
mitigations: Disable shared folders between the agents.
Route inter-agent exchange through a strict JSON schema.
Add provenance tags to every file passed between agents.
Require manual review before any MCP/tool output is re-used.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation at the orchestrator layer.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches source code and files in cwd with broad network egress; Agent B touches documents, notes, files, API keys, and persistent memory with broad egress and many external connectors. If they share a workspace, sensitive material from B can be read by A and then exfiltrated through either agent's network paths. The pairwise leakage pathway is therefore strong.
conditions: IF both agents access the same directory or mounted volume, B's files can be exposed to A.
IF either agent forwards retrieved file contents to external APIs, leakage can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces.
Remove secrets from any shared directory.
Turn off network egress for one agent during sensitive tasks.
Use per-agent service accounts and API keys.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP/redaction before any outbound call.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can write the filesystem and modify git state; Agent B can access local files and mounted volumes and also run subprocesses with broad egress. In a shared repo or volume, concurrent writes and git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt state. The profiles do not mention locking, so conflict risk is high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout, concurrent commits or edits can conflict.
IF both agents write to the same mounted volume, file corruption or lost updates can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Serialize write access with a simple lock file.
Pause one agent while the other performs git operations.
Use read-only mounts for one agent.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can generate code, shell actions, and MCP outputs; Agent B can consume files, documents, and tool outputs in a persistent web app session. That makes it plausible for B to treat A's output as authoritative and propagate mistakes into downstream artifacts or actions. The blast radius is meaningful but not inherently irreversible from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF Agent B uses Agent A's output without verification, errors can cascade into later outputs.
IF Agent A emits malformed code or facts that B republishes, the mistake propagates.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before B acts on A's output.
Require B to cite source files for any claims from A.
Use a validation script on A's outputs.
Limit A to draft-only mode.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B explicitly handles documents, notes, calendar events, persistent memory, usage analytics, and API keys, while Agent A handles source code and files in cwd. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into B's persistent web app and then moved through A's broad filesystem/network surface, retention and residency controls may diverge. The profiles do not document matching compliance controls, so this is a medium mismatch risk.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in Agent B's persistent memory, retention obligations may be violated.
IF EU or PHI data is routed through Agent A's broad egress without a DPA or residency control, compliance exposure increases.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workflows.
Disable persistent memory for sensitive sessions.
Use region-locked deployments and documented DPAs.
Separate logs by agent and retention class.
requires-engineering: map data flows to compliance controls before deployment.
